article.articleHeadline: Socioeconomic vulnerability associated with schistosomiasis in indigenous communities of southern Brazil
article.articleSummary: Schistosomiasis, a snail-borne neglected tropical disease caused by Schistosoma mansoni, was evaluated in six indigenous communities in southern Brazil (n=412) and four in southeastern Brazil (n=301). Among 713 individuals, overall seropositivity for anti-S. mansoni antibodies (IgM and/or IgG) was 5.3% (38/713; 95% CI 3.9–7.2). Seroprevalence was 5.8% in the southern region (24/412) and 4.7% in the southeastern region (14/301), with no statistical difference between regions. Among seropositive individuals, IgM predominated (33/38; 86.8%) versus IgG (10/38; 26.3%), suggesting recent infection. Univariate associations included drinking river water and open-pit fecal disposal; however, final logistic regression retained community location/characteristic as the associated variable. The findings support ongoing schistosomiasis surveillance in low-endemic areas, particularly in indigenous communities serving as environmental sentinels of pathogen distribution.

article.articleHeadline: Hidden Parasite Split: DNA Reveals Snake Coccidia on the Brink of Becoming
article.articleSummary: DNA analyses reclassify Caryospora jararacae, a coccidian parasite of venomous snakes, within a newly defined species complex spanning five continents. In Rio de Janeiro’s Atlantic Forest, Brazilian researchers collected fecal samples from five Bothrops jararaca and five Crotalus durissus rescued in Miguel Pereira. Oocysts appeared in 60% of jararacas and 80% of rattlesnakes (overall 70%). Morphology showed subspheroidal oocysts ~14×14 μm with a bi-layered wall, Stieda and sub-Stieda bodies. Four non-overlapping loci—three mitochondrial (MAVCOXI, MARI, MACOIII) and nuclear 18S—were sequenced. Brazilian parasites matched Caryospora bigenetica, with 100% identity at 18S, 97.7–99.3% at mitochondrial loci, and 99% across the concatenated dataset. Bayesian and maximum-likelihood trees strongly support a monophyletic clade (PP 0.99, bootstrap 100%). The work confirms Caryospora jararacae as distinct from prior Brazilian records and highlights a broader evolutionary split in snake coccidia, across a five-continental complex.

article.articleHeadline: In Philippines, woman's arm and leg start shaking, then MRI reveals suspected worm eggs
article.articleSummary: Suspected neuroschistosomiasis due to Schistosoma japonicum diagnosed after a Philippine woman experienced a sudden minute-long episode of shaking in her right arm and leg; MRI showed a bright cluster of nodules with surrounding fluid in the left frontal lobe, prompting suspicion of brain-lodged worm eggs. S. japonicum, the most common blood fluke in the Philippines, is found in the Philippines, China, and parts of Indonesia (now absent in Japan). The parasite's life cycle begins when eggs shed in urine or feces reach water, infect snails, which release cercariae that penetrate unbroken skin and migrate through the lungs, heart, and liver before maturing. Eggs trapped in tissue trigger inflammation and organ-specific damage; adult worms may persist in vessels without symptoms. The case adds to reports of snail-borne infections elsewhere, including rat lungworm in California and related concerns in Europe and Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: A parasite invades horses' brains and leaves researchers on the lookout - Boca do Povo News
article.articleSummary: Two Criollo horses in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, were studied after a rare parasite invaded the nervous system in 2021 and 2023. The nematode Halicephalobus gingivalis was detected in nervous tissue and other organs; histology showed inflammation and larvae near blood vessels, while rabies tests were negative. Genetic analysis placed the Brazilian isolates in Lineage 3, the same lineage as samples from other countries, providing a molecular identifier for these cases. The parasite normally inhabits the environment and rarely infects mammals, but central nervous system involvement can be fatal, leading to euthanasia in both cases due to irreversibility. Although the episodes occurred on different properties with almost two years between them, the study found no evidence the Criollo breed is more susceptible. Clinicians and breeders should monitor for sudden neurological changes and seek veterinary care, recognizing that such symptoms have multiple potential causes.

article.articleHeadline: Leprosy is increasing in the country.
article.articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) is rising in India. All 31 states/UTs have reached the 1 per 10,000 elimination target, except five states—Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Odisha—and one UT above it. article.articleHeadline: Drones Broaden the Municipalities' View in the Fight Against Dengue
article.articleSummary: Drone-based aerial mapping enhances dengue control by enabling precise territory surveillance and faster, targeted interventions. By linking mapped points to precise locations, managers can plan field visits and allocate resources where needed. article.articleHeadline: Hidden Tick- and Flea-Borne Probes in HIV Patients Reveal High Bartonella
article.articleSummary: In Brazil, a cross-sectional study of 75 symptomatic HIV-positive individuals found 62.7% had seroreactivity to Bartonella antigens (most frequently B. henselae, 57.3%; B. vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii II, 44%). Despite serology, molecular testing—qPCR and digital PCR on blood samples with up to 28 days of BAPGM enrichment—detected no Bartonella or Borrelia DNA in any participant. Two participants showed low-positive piroplasmid DNA by dPCR. Clinically, 11 seroreactive patients had systemic manifestations versus 1 non-seroreactive (odds ratio 8.25; 95% CI 1.00–68.2; p = 0.026). Authors note serology may reflect prior exposure, cross-reactivity, or low-level colonization rather than active infection. No active Bartonella or Borrelia infection was demonstrated; the study raises questions about the infectious status of Bartonella exposure in HIV patients in a tropical setting, with potential implications for diagnosis and surveillance.

Residents question whether municipal health authorities’ negligence could trigger a major outbreak and have demanded immediate bin cleaning and regular fumigation/disinfection. They argue that surface cleaning is insufficient; proper sanitation and routine insecticide spraying at bin sites are essential. If an outbreak occurs, accountability remains disputed, and residents urge authorities to urgently sanitize and disinfect the waste bins to mitigate public health risk.

article.articleHeadline: Hidden Mycobacteria in Cattle Carry Genes Linked to Drug Resistance
article.articleSummary: India (Ludhiana) study of bovine non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTMs) from cattle and buffaloes examined 193 clinical samples (101 feces, 21 nasal swabs, 13 transtracheal washes, 30 tissues, 28 blood). Using direct PCR and culture-based isolation, 18 NTMs were confirmed after hsp65 genus screening and species-level PCR. Mycobacterium vaccae dominated (66.7% of isolates). The team screened four resistance-associated genes—rpoB (rifampicin), katG (isoniazid), rpsL (streptomycin), and gyrA (fluoroquinolones). rpoB was detected in 88.9% of isolates (primarily M. vaccae), katG in 16.7%, gyrA in 5.6%, while rpsL was not amplified. Findings fill a gap in Indian bovine NTM resistance data and have implications for diagnostic interpretation and bovine TB surveillance, highlighting environmental mycobacteria as common bovine associates.

article.articleHeadline: 3,832 Child Leprosy Cases Challenge India's 2027 Goal
article.articleSummary: India reported 3,832 new child leprosy cases in 2025–26, 91.6% above the target of 2,000, signaling ongoing transmission. Thirty-seven newly diagnosed children had Grade-2 disability at detection, indicating nerve or eye damage before diagnosis. Across all ages, 91,783 new leprosy cases were reported in 2025–26; children accounted for 4.18%, and 1,945 patients had Grade-2 disability at detection. Leprosy (Hansen disease) is mainly skin and peripheral nerves; transmission is believed to occur via droplets from prolonged close contact with untreated cases. Multidrug therapy with rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine is given for six to twelve months, depending on classification. A district is considered to have interrupted transmission after five consecutive years with no new indigenous child cases; India targets this by 2027. Despite national elimination in 2005, prevalence fell to 0.57 per 10,000 in 2025, yet tens of thousands of new cases continue yearly.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies and the missing deaths: Why do India's official numbers differ so sharply from estimates? |Explained
article.articleSummary: India aims to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 but lacks a single national death tally. IDSP-IHIP logged 54 human rabies deaths in 2024; 21 in 2022 and 50 in 2023. The Registrar General's MCCD counted 66 deaths in 2022 and 271 in 2023, but these are medically certified deaths and cover only a fraction of totals. Rabies is not nationally notifiable, though the NCDC is pushing states to notify under their laws; many deaths occur outside formal health systems, hampering surveillance. In four months of 2026, Tamil Nadu recorded 2.63 lakh dog bites and 17 rabies deaths. A Lancet Infectious Diseases study led by ICMR estimates about 5,726 deaths in India, derived from a large community survey (337,808 people in 60 districts across 15 states) and a probability model; about 9.1 million animal bites yearly (including 5.6 million dog bites). The gap arises from differing surveillance, certification, and model-based approaches.

article.articleHeadline: Rise of falciparum malaria: if left untreated, kidneys and brain may fail. How to stay vigilant?
article.articleSummary: Falciparum malaria, the most dangerous malaria parasite (Plasmodium falciparum), has been detected in Mumbai and across several locations in India during the monsoon season, with climate-driven mosquito proliferation implicated by WHO researchers. If untreated, this malaria can cause cerebral malaria, coma, or death. The disease is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes; four human Plasmodium species exist—vivax, falciparum, ovale, and malariae—with P. falciparum causing malignant malaria. Symptoms include sudden high fever with chills, persistent elevated temperature, severe headache, muscle cramps, diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal bloating; the parasite destroys red blood cells, causing anemia. In the brain, disrupted blood flow can lead to unconsciousness or coma. Prevention focuses on eliminating standing water, using mosquito nets in high-risk areas, and keeping surroundings clean; fever persisting three days warrants a blood test.

article.articleHeadline: Threatening Dengue Fever.. How to Protect Yourself?
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever remains a major concern in Tamil Nadu’s Chennai Corporation area, with 4,592 dengue infections reported this year, alongside typhoid and other viral fevers. Emergency measures and dedicated medical camps aim to curb spread and provide timely care, contributing to a gradual decline in cases. Most patients are managing illness at home; only about 5–10% require intensive medical supervision. Public vigilance is crucial to prevent transmission, since the Aedes aegypti mosquito can bite during the day and spread the infection to others if not controlled. Protective actions include covering arms and legs, using safe repellents, keeping doors and windows screened, and employing mosquito coils or electric devices when mosquitoes are prevalent. If dengue is present nearby, cleaning and maintaining surroundings is essential; eliminating standing water in the neighborhood reduces risk for all residents.

article.articleHeadline: Meningitis risk in young children; do not delay treatment even for a moment; risk of death - Agra
article.articleSummary: Agra, 2026-10-05 — Viral meningitis in children and TB-related meningitis are rising, with affected youngsters admitted in government and private hospitals in serious condition. On Meningitis Day, doctors at SN Medical College & Hospital in Agra urged timely diagnosis and treatment to prevent deaths. Emergency department screenings show about 5% of children presenting with loss of consciousness have meningitis. Pediatrician Dr. Neeraj Yadav explains that in children under five, viral and bacterial infections, along with brain coverings inflammation, reduce brain oxygen and trigger seizures, high fever, headache, vomiting, and sometimes unconsciousness. Delayed treatment can be fatal; survivors may suffer paralysis, and TB meningitis increases this risk. Preventive steps include vaccinations (BCG, meningococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and pneumococcal), hygiene, and nutritious meals to strengthen immunity. Seek immediate medical care for fever with seizures or altered consciousness.

article.articleHeadline: India's top killer diseases have changed, but TB and infections still won't go away
article.articleSummary: WHO Global Health Estimates (2000–2023) show India’s biggest killer in 2023 is ischaemic heart disease at 138.5 deaths per 100,000, followed by stroke (74.8), COPD (83.19) and diabetes (49.01). The shift from 2000 is stark: TB (92.4) and diarrhoeal diseases (87.8) led mortality then. Infections persist: TB, diarrhoeal diseases and lower respiratory infections remain among the top 10 causes, alongside cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. Diarrhoeal deaths declined markedly—from about 1.46 million in 1990 to 462,220 in 2023, with a crude death rate of 32/100,000—thanks to sanitation, safe water, vaccination and treatment access. TB remains a major challenge globally and in India. A GBD 2023 analysis notes COPD, ischaemic heart disease and stroke as large contributors to tobacco-attributable deaths in India. By 2023, non-communicable diseases account for ~75% of top-10 deaths ( communicable ~16%), while road injuries rank 10th with ~174,000 deaths (about 14% of roughly 12.2 lakh global road deaths).

article.articleHeadline: Uttar Pradesh to Run Communicable Disease Control and Dastak Campaigns in October
article.articleSummary: Uttar Pradesh will conduct a Special Communicable Disease Control Campaign from October 1–31, 2026, followed by the Dastak Campaign from October 12–31. The initiatives center on public awareness, cleanliness, symptom identification, and timely treatment. Health workers, ASHA workers, Anganwadi workers and staff from other departments will visit households across the state to engage residents, disseminate information on cleanliness, recognizing symptoms, and seeking prompt care. The household-level outreach aims to strengthen awareness of communicable diseases and promote preventive and medical actions. The Dastak Campaign overlaps with the broader Special Campaign from October 12 onward. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath cited the elimination of encephalitis in eastern Uttar Pradesh as evidence that coordinated efforts and public participation can achieve major public-health gains. The campaigns emphasize prevention, early identification, and timely treatment, combining administrative measures with community involvement to protect public health in October.

article.articleHeadline: Is there itching on your body? It’s not an infection—these could be the symptoms of this serious disease. Don’t ignore them; find out immediately.
article.articleSummary: Shingles (herpes zoster), caused by the Varicella-Zoster virus, reactivates from latent nerve cells after chickenpox. It presents as a painful rash and vesicles on one side of the body, following a dermatomal path, with burning, stinging, itching, and pain; crusting occurs in a few days and most lesions heal in 2-4 weeks. A key complication is postherpetic neuralgia, persisting pain in about 10-18% of cases, more common with age. Facial or periorbital involvement can affect vision; rare cases can cause encephalitis. Studies link shingles to higher risk of stroke and other heart-vascular events, especially in the early days/weeks after infection, possibly via vasculopathy. Prevention in India emphasizes vaccination to prevent reactivation and severe pain. If a household member has shingles, avoid direct contact with lesions and keep them clean and covered; seek medical care promptly to manage symptoms and reduce complications.

article.articleHeadline: Scabies: The invisible skin infection that is more than skin-deep
article.articleSummary: Scabies, caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, remains a neglected tropical disease in India, disproportionately affecting marginalized communities from Baiga Adivasis in Chhattisgarh to Kondh tribals in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and the labouring poor of Bihar and Gujarat. Budhram, a 12-year-old at a Baiga residential school in Chhattisgarh, and his mother and siblings endure relentless itching, sleepless nights and social hardship; local injections provide partial relief at high cost. Transmission is via close contact, with outbreaks in dormitories, hospitals, prisons and refugee camps; reinfection is common due to unwashed clothes and bedding, limited water, and overcrowding. Globally, Global Burden of Disease 2021 data report about 206.6 million people infected at any time and roughly 622.5 million new cases annually. In 2017, WHO designated scabies a Neglected Tropical Disease. Control requires mass community treatment: boiling clothes, distributing extra garments, applying antiscabies lotion, and providing tablets and antibiotics, with strong community participation.

article.articleHeadline: Nipah-Ebola spreads from 'Na Manush', headache and dengue too! Now district-by-district One Health Committees across the state.
article.articleSummary: As of 5 October 2026, the state is establishing district-by-district One Health Committees to curb cross-species disease spread, spotlighting Nipah and Ebola linked to 'Na Manush,' and noting dengue. One Health requires coordination among veterinarians, environmental specialists, local administration, and food-safety officers to monitor infection sources and vectors in animals and the environment, not just treat humans. The new committees will include district magistrates, chief medical officers, Deputy Director of the Animal Resources Development Department, the district medical college principal, divisional forest officer, veterinary laboratory in-charge, municipal officer, district panchayat president, and rural development officer, forming multidisciplinary teams at every district. Professor Siddharth Joarder of the State Veterinary and Fisheries University backs the plan, citing Nipah from fruit bats and rising antibiotic resistance as concerns; the approach aligns with WHO, OIE, FAO, and UNEP initiatives that stress integrated health beyond borders after SARS, MERS, Ebola, and COVID-19.

In the drive, Lakshmipuram Primary Health Centre administered chloroquine to 71 people; at least five malaria cases had been reported in the village. article.articleHeadline: Flooded Faizullahganj: Water-borne diseases' risk spikes; health staff on alert
article.articleSummary: Flooding in Faizullahganj raises the risk of water‑borne diseases such as diarrhoea, hepatitis A, cholera and typhoid from contaminated water and food, with leptospirosis, skin and respiratory infections, and snakebite also monitored. The health department has intensified surveillance and preparedness, conducting household health surveys in Faizullaganj led by Dr Asma with ASHAs and ANMs, and deploying mobile medical units to flood‑affected areas. Hospitals have reserved beds to manage potential increases: 10 beds at Ram Sagar Mishra Hospital and 10 beds at Bhau Rao Devras Hospital, along with adequate stocks of medicines and anti-snake venom. Officials, including Dr Kuldeep Verma and Dr NB Singh, emphasize floodwater carries dirt, microorganisms and insecticides contributing to illness. The district health office reports multiple medical teams and MMUs; centers are instructed to maintain essential medicines during the crisis.

article.articleHeadline: Punjab to intensify Hepatitis C screening, strengthen transfusion safety
article.articleSummary: Punjab will intensify Hepatitis C screening and bolster transfusion safety, targeting a lower Hepatitis C positivity rate through rigorous screening, early treatment linkage, comprehensive tracking, and strict blood-safety protocols. Punjab maintains 198 licensed blood centres (49 government, 7 military, 142 private/trust); in 2025-26, 5,44,167 units were collected across 6,583 camps, with government centres contributing 1,78,382 units, of which 1,77,583 (about 99.6%) came from voluntary donors. Four focal areas aim to transform transfusion services and healthcare, including motivating youth to donate and transitioning from ‘Star Donors’ to ‘Star Motivators.’ Districts Patiala and Sangrur were best performers; Pathankot is a Saksham District; Fazilka, Muktsar, Amritsar, Kapurla, Mohali and Bathinda named Surakshit Districts. article.articleHeadline: Chigger-Borne Scrub Typhus Showed Up as Muscle Spasms in an Unusual Case, and the Kidneys May Be to Blame
article.articleSummary: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi), transmitted by chiggers, presented unusually in AIIMS Hyderabad as tetany from hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia, likely due to renal tubular electrolyte loss. The July 2026 Tropical Doctor case report notes the abstract omits age, labs, treatment, and outcome, but calls this a potentially under-recognized metabolic manifestation. Kidney involvement is a known complication; CDC lists kidney or liver failure and other severe outcomes after the first week if untreated. Classic signs are often missing; eschar can be present in as little as 1% to as high as 97% depending on region. In Pondicherry, India, a pediatric series found eschar in 31.6%, rash 7.2%, lymphadenopathy 93.5%, hyponatremia 16.5%, with no deaths. No vaccine exists; doxycycline is the recommended treatment. In the US, Orientia was detected in chiggers in North Carolina parks in 2023, but no human cases.

article.articleHeadline: Study Reveals Shared Inflammation in Biliary Atresia and COVID-19
article.articleSummary: Biliary atresia and SARS-CoV-2–associated liver injury share antiviral defenses, double-stranded RNA responses, and interferon signaling in bile duct cells. Harbin, China–based researchers compared SARS-CoV-2–infected human liver organoids with biliary atresia liver tissue, identifying 164 shared genes and narrowing to 52 after stringent testing. Key genes STAT1, ISG15, and CXCL10 remained prominent; cholangiocytes (bile duct lining cells) showed higher activation of the shared pattern in COVID-associated liver samples (P = 0.00368). An independent biliary atresia dataset showed elevated expression of these genes in cholangiocytes. In vitro, synthetic dsRNA increased these genes and proteins, with CXCL10 showing the strongest rise. Mefloquine emerged as a potential candidate for further study, though no proven efficacy. Published in Frontiers in Immunology (2026), the findings suggest shared inflammatory stress responses across distinct liver diseases, warranting larger follow-up studies.

article.articleHeadline: New Infectivity Atlas Maps Which Sarbecoviruses Can Latch Onto Human and
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-10-05, investigators mapped infectivity for 46 sarbecoviruses against 66 ACE2 orthologs (48 bat-derived from 11 families) using pseudotyped vesicular stomatitis virus with spike proteins and luminescent entry readouts, producing a cross-species infectivity heatmap. Phylogeny divides viruses into clade 1 (1a: SARS-CoV-1 relatives; 1b: SARS-CoV-2 relatives, including RaTG13 and pangolin viruses), clade 2 (majority with a double RBM deletion and ACE2-independent entry), and clade 3 (BtKY72, Khosta-2). Clade 1b pangolin viruses PCoV-GD and PCoV-GX show broad ACE2 compatibility, infecting most non-bat mammalian ACE2s; RaTG13 exhibits a restricted host range despite high spike similarity to SARS-CoV-2. WIV1 (bat) bridges human and bat ACE2 usage. Clade 2 viruses do not use ACE2; Clade 3 species show limited to modest ACE2 usage. Across all 46 viruses, none of NRP1, CD147, AXL, TMEM106B supported infection, reinforcing ACE2 as the primary entry receptor. The study identifies two bat species with human-like ACE2 receptors, flagging them for surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Endothelial Angptl2 Emerges as Central Driver of Influenza-Linked Lung
article.articleSummary: Influenza-associated pulmonary fibrosis is driven by endothelial Angptl2. In Hangzhou, China, researchers at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine linked vascular Angptl2 to fibrotic remodeling using human transcriptomics, a murine H1N1 model, and single-cell sequencing. Angptl2 expression rises in endothelial cells during disease and is elevated in bronchoalveolar lavage from fibrotic patients versus non-fibrotic controls. In Angptl2 knockout mice, fibrosis is attenuated with preserved lung architecture and reduced extracellular matrix. Mechanistically, Angptl2 binds the α5β1 integrin on endothelial cells, activating MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling to promote endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT). EndMT cells secrete endothelin-1, triggering NF-κB activation in neighboring fibroblasts to become matrix-producing. A protective Rgs2-positive endothelial population expands in Angptl2-deficient mice, suggesting Angptl2 normally suppresses this state. Findings reveal a vascular-endothelial axis linking acute viral injury to chronic scarring and highlight potential therapeutic targets.

article.articleHeadline: Agenda-setting relations between Chinese state media reports and public social media posts: focusing on COVID-19
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 coverage in China shows divergent agenda patterns for state media (People’s Daily) versus social media (Weibo) across four periods. In the imminent period, People’s Daily linked infection-status updates with official directives and Wuhan-related notifications, while Weibo centered on exploratory signals and uncertainty. In the current period, People’s Daily shifted toward crisis management and resource mobilization at the national level; Weibo focused on Wuhan’s outbreak, patient treatment, and regional spread. In the critical period, People’s Daily integrated international coordination, interregional experience sharing, and standardized data releases, producing a coherent governance-oriented network; Weibo emphasized official statistics, press briefings, suspected-case responses, and overseas developments, maintaining information transmission. During the dormant period, People’s Daily broadened to global response, economic consequences, and post-outbreak policy objectives, whereas Weibo remained oriented to routine testing and provincial updates. As of 2026-10-05, comparative analysis highlights governance-embedded versus monitoring-oriented infection-status agendas across the COVID-19 issue cycle.

article.articleHeadline: Two cases of veterans' illness recorded in Hong Kong in one week
article.articleSummary: Two cases of Legionnaires' disease were recorded in Hong Kong from Sep 27 to Oct 3, 2026, comprising a 67-year-old man in the Southern District with community-acquired infection and a 55-year-old woman who had traveled to Mainland China during the incubation period, classified as imported. As of Oct 3, 2026, Hong Kong's total is 153 cases this year. Authorities say these are sporadic with no epidemiological link to earlier HK cases. Historical totals: 2025, 167 cases; 2024, 135. Risk factors include male sex, age over 50, smoking, alcohol use, and immunocompromise. Environmental sources include poorly maintained water systems, hot-water systems, cooling towers, spas, fountains, humidifiers, and home medical equipment. article.articleHeadline: Weather and Pollution Show Little Sway Over Respiratory Pathogens in
article.articleSummary: Kaifeng, Henan Province, China, hosted a retrospective BMC Infectious Diseases study at a sentinel hospital (2023–2025) testing 17 common respiratory pathogens by real-time quantitative PCR in 1,716 patients. Of these, 957 (55.77%) were positive for at least one pathogen; viruses accounted for 40.44% and bacteria 28.03%. Most infections involved a single organism (34.15%), but 21.51% were mixed infections. Children bore the heaviest burden (69.81% positivity) versus adults aged 66+ (35.68%), with negligible sex differences. Urban residents had markedly higher positivity (62.10%) than rural residents (20.28%). Seasonality was evident: Influenza A peaked in winter (20.40%), Rhinovirus in autumn (15.63%). Early environmental correlations included a negative association for influenza B with precipitation (r_s = -0.591, p<0.05) and a positive association for Bordetella pertussis with PM2.5 (r_s = 0.597, p<0.05). The study notes cautious interpretation as weather and pollution links are explored; published 2026-10-05.

article.articleHeadline: They may cause cancer: Scientists clearly pointed to dangerous viruses and a bacterium.
article.articleSummary: Globally in 2024, infections caused about 2.3 million cancers, 12% of all new cancers; Helicobacter pylori responsible ~760,000 cases and HPV ~750,000; HBV 360,000; EBV 260,000; HCV 160,000. H. pylori mainly non-cardia gastric cancer; HPV mainly cervical cancer. Other pathogens include KSHV, HTLV-1, MCV, HIV and three parasites. EBV infection common but cancer develops in a small subset; EBV linked to some stomach cancers and certain lymphomas. Prevention is feasible: HPV and HBV vaccines; H. pylori treatable with antibiotics; HCV curable with antivirals; HIV/HBV/HCV testing and treatment; safe injection practices; condoms; PrEP. 2024 regional distribution: East Asia ~990k cases (42% globally); Sub-Saharan Africa 25%; LMICs account for 77% of infections-related cancers. Emphasizes prevention and access to care worldwide.

article.articleHeadline: Dr. Jiruruj warns Korat of flu outbreak; one child has died; reveals dangerous signs; you must rush your child to the hospital.
article.articleSummary: On 5 October 2026, Dr. Jiruruj Chomchai, a pediatric respiratory and critical-care specialist at Maharaj Nakorn Ratchasima Hospital, warned of a continuing influenza outbreak in Nakhon Ratchasima Province (Korat), Thailand, where one death has occurred: a roughly 7-year-old overweight child with no major comorbidities. Flu cases can lead to severe complications in children. Red flags requiring urgent hospital care include: rapid or labored breathing with chest retractions; cyanosis; severe dehydration (no urination for 8 hours, dry mouth, absent tears); altered mental status or seizures; severe muscle pain hindering movement; fever >40°C despite antipyretics; and fever in infants under 3 months. High-risk groups should receive antivirals promptly (e.g., Oseltamivir): obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile); age under 5 (especially under 2); chronic conditions (asthma, heart, lung, kidney, liver, blood disorders, diabetes); neurological/developmental disorders; immunodeficiencies (HIV on ART, cancer, chronic steroids). Outbreak persists in urban and district areas; schools may close around 6 October.

article.articleHeadline: Head Lice in Thai Schools Carry Mutations Linked to Pyrethroid Resistance
article.articleSummary: Head lice infestation (Pediculus humanus capitis) in eastern Thailand's Chonburi Province shows emerging pyrethroid resistance. In a May–July 2024 survey of 960 schoolchildren across five public schools, overall pediculosis prevalence was 20.42% (95% CI 17.91–23.11%), higher in rural than urban settings. Logistic regression linked infestation with sex, school level, hair length, and reported pediculicide use, suggesting possible cycles of treatment failure or rapid reinfestation. Molecular analyses confirmed lice identity and placed samples in mitochondrial clades A or C. Crucially, knockdown resistance mutations in the voltage-gated sodium channel gene—T917I and L920F—were detected, with homozygous resistant genotypes found in lice from four schools, indicating established pyrethroid resistance in local populations. Resistant lice were found in children with and without reported permethrin treatment history, implying community-wide circulation. Findings published in Parasites & Vectors.

article.articleHeadline: Deutsche Welle: The Sindbis fever virus from the Egyptian village Sindbis infects the first person in Germany!
article.articleSummary: Germany reports the first laboratory-confirmed Sindbis fever case in Baden-Württemberg. A 60-year-old man from Stuttgart was infected on 12 July; the infection was confirmed in September 2026 by the Robert Koch Institute, and he is recovering without symptoms. The case indicates local Sindbis virus circulation in Germany, with previous undetected infections found among Weinheim blood donors. Sindbis virus primarily infects birds and is transmitted by mosquitoes; it does not spread human-to-human. It is found across Eurasia and Africa; disease is usually mild or asymptomatic, but can cause fever, itchy rash, and joint pain, with arthritis lasting months in some cases. No specific antiviral treatment exists; care is supporting. Clinicians should consider Sindbis during mosquito season for febrile patients with rash and arthralgia, even without travel. Isolation was in 1952 in Egypt's Nile Delta, named after Sindbis village; human cases occurred in Uganda (1961), South Africa (1963), Australia (1967).

article.articleHeadline: Two Mpox Clades Now Circulate in Pakistan, Genomic Surveillance Reveals

Of 137 suspected cases, 29 were RT-PCR confirmed; four high-viral-load samples were sequenced on Illumina iSeq. cohort: median age 31 (range 0.6–80); 68.9% male, 27.6% female, 3.4% transgender. Imported infections 44.8% (n=13); secondary 17.2% (n=5); locally acquired 20.7% (n=6); probable local 17.2% (n=5). Phylogeny shows links to sequences from Pakistan, the United States, Nepal and Thailand, indicating international travel–driven seeding amid labor migration.

article.articleHeadline: Assessment of the zoonotic spillover potential of SARS-CoV-2-related coronaviruses from Rhinolophus pusillus bats in Thailand
article.articleSummary: In Ratchaburi, Thailand, 261 Rhinolophus pusillus bats carried coronaviruses at a 16.47% prevalence, including SARS-CoV-2–related lineages. Five complete SARS-CoV-2–related coronavirus genomes were recovered, with one, RpuRB21065, showing high spike and receptor-binding domain similarity to SARS-CoV-2. The RBD bound human ACE2, and the spike protein induced syncytia in vitro. However, sera from SARS-CoV-2–vaccinated individuals effectively neutralized RpuRB21065, suggesting pre-existing SARS-CoV-2 immunity may mitigate current spillover risk. The study serves as proof-of-concept that proactive wildlife surveillance in emerging infectious disease hotspots can yield information with direct public health relevance, even without viral isolation. Findings underscore the value of wildlife monitoring at human–wildlife interfaces in informing pandemic risk assessment in Thailand and similar settings, without reporting any human cases at this time.

article.articleHeadline: Spatial-temporal heterogeneity in tuberculosis incidence and its association with socioeconomic factors in South Sulawesi
article.articleSummary: TB remains a major public health challenge in Indonesia; this study analyzes tuberculosis incidence in South Sulawesi across 24 districts from 2018–2023. Reported TB incidence varied markedly between districts with an overall upward trend and widening disparities, and high-burden areas shifted over time rather than persisting. Districts frequently reclassified across incidence categories, indicating unstable patterns. Global Moran's I suggested no consistent spatial clustering, while the Breusch-Pagan test showed strong spatial heterogeneity. Using a Nonparametric Geographically and Temporally Weighted Regression with Truncated Spline (NGTWR-TS), researchers found nonlinear threshold effects and substantial spatial-temporal variation in how socioeconomic conditions relate to incidence. Consistent correlates included mean years of schooling, open unemployment rate, and the Human Development Index, all positively associated with district CIR. The results imply district-specific interventions addressing education, employment, and development to counter dynamic, localized vulnerabilities in TB incidence as of 2023; implications for policy in South Sulawesi.

article.articleHeadline: aespa's Winter Contracted Herpes Zoster! What Is That Disease?
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-10-05, aespa member Winter has been diagnosed with herpes zoster (shingles) following a hospital examination. Herpes zoster results from reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox, remaining latent after infection and reactivating with age or immune compromise. Symptoms include unilateral pain, itching, tingling, or numbness, followed by a vesicular rash that crusts; fever, headache, chills, and fatigue may occur. The condition is not directly contagious, but blister fluid can spread varicella-zoster to someone who has not had chickenpox or vaccination, potentially causing chickenpox. Treatment involves antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) and pain management; patients should cover lesions and maintain hygiene. No case counts or outbreak details provided.

article.articleHeadline: 5 Hidden Places in the Home That Could Be Breeding Grounds for Dengue-Carrying Mosquitoes, Check Now.
article.articleSummary: Hidden indoor spots can breed dengue-carrying mosquitoes, even in seemingly clean homes. A VNExpress report (5 Oct 2026) notes small amounts of standing water can accumulate unnoticed, sustaining the dengue vector. Five locations to inspect: 1) drip trays under appliances such as refrigerators, portable air conditioners, dehumidifiers, and water dispensers; empty and clean removable trays at least weekly and check for leaks. 2) Flower vases, plant containers, and saucers; replace vase water regularly, clean the containers, and pour away water from saucers after watering; eggs can cling to old water lines, so avoid overwatering. 3) Buckets, containers, and rarely used items; even bottle caps, cups, or loose bags can hold rainwater; store unused items in sheltered or inverted positions and discard what’s unnecessary. 4) Gutters, balconies, and roofs; debris can clog channels, causing pooling; inspect after rain, clean drains, secure covers, and address pools with professionals if needed.

article.articleHeadline: Preparation for Hajj and Umrah, Pilgrims Urged to Be Wary of Pneumonia Risk
article.articleSummary: Pneumonia risk for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims, especially older adults and those with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or stroke, is emphasized in Pfizer Indonesia’s 'Lindungi Napasmu, Jaga Momen Berarti' campaign. A YouGov survey of Muslim respondents shows 43% plan to perform Hajj/Umrah within two years, with crowded conditions increasing exposure to respiratory infections. Only 11% recognise crowds as a source of risk for serious pneumonia. Pneumococcal pneumonia, caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, differs from influenza, though both affect the respiratory tract; upper respiratory infections can progress to pneumonia. Risks during the pilgrimage include fatigue from long flights, jet lag, climate changes, dehydration, and comorbidity. Recommendations: adequate rest, hydration, handwashing, and masking in crowded places, plus medical check-ups about six months before departure following government guidelines. Clinicians highlight controlling chronic conditions to reduce pneumonia risk in Saudi Arabia’s Mecca and Medina and on return to Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: A Mild Cough That Turned Out to Be Tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Tuberculosis (TB) can present with mild symptoms; a case involved a three-month faint cough with no fever or weight loss, leading to a TB diagnosis. The piece stresses that many TB patients have light early symptoms and delay seeking care, heightening lung damage and the risk of spreading the disease. A simple rule: a cough lasting more than two weeks should be evaluated, regardless of perceived severity. TB can exist as latent infection—no symptoms and not contagious—but can reactivate if immunity weakens (uncontrolled diabetes, HIV, malnutrition, smoking). Indonesia ranks second globally for TB after India, with about 1.1 million new cases in 2024, roughly 10% of global cases, and WHO notes a sizable gap between estimated and detected cases. TB is airborne, not transmitted through shared dishes. After diagnosis, treatment requires regular medication adherence and precautions (e.g., masking) to prevent transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Filariasis Cases Cluster Near Mosquito Breeding Grounds on Indonesian
article.articleSummary: On Belitung Island, Indonesia, lymphatic filariasis persists despite mass drug administration. A 2019 cross-sectional survey in Suak Gual (Selat Nasik Subdistrict) and Lasar (Membalong Subdistrict; sub-villages Batumana, Dudat, Ulin) enrolled 671 residents to assess Brugia malayi–driven disease, diagnosed via nocturnal thick blood smears collected after dark. Researchers geolocated homes and mapped water bodies with Mansonia mosquito breeding habitat (macrophyte-rich, floating vegetation in swamps/ponds). Spatial analyses showed strong clustering of infections near such habitats: Clark-Evans R=0.380, p<0.001 in Suak Gual; R=0.432, p<0.001 in Batumana. Ulin showed weaker association (R=0.654, p=0.026) that did not survive Bonferroni correction; Dudat (R=0.856, p=0.434) showed no significant clustering. Findings, published in Acta Parasitologica, suggest integrating habitat-targeted vector control with ongoing or renewed mass drug administration to reduce transmission and prevent recrudescence.

article.articleHeadline: Dug Wells and Crowded Cities: New Model Maps Fecal Contamination Risk in
article.articleSummary: Nearly 95 million urban Indonesians draw part of drinking water from groundwater; about 68% lack safely managed drinking water. Among households using self-supplied groundwater as their main source, E. coli was detected in 69% of samples, and 21.2% exceeded the WHO high-risk threshold of 100 CFU/100 mL, a contamination linked to a 54% higher risk of diarrhea. Using a source–pathway–receptor framework calibrated to the SKAM-RT 2020 survey (21,829 households; 847 with dug-wells/boreholes; 619 analyzed), the study built a nationwide risk ranking to map microbial contamination risk. Four predictors remained: water source type (dug-wells vs drilled boreholes) with dug-wells at 2.9× higher odds of high E. coli, aquifer lithology, rainfall in months prior, and population density. Locations underlain by solid/volcanic rock showed ~40% lower odds than unconsolidated sediment or limestone. This work offers a cost-effective screening tool to focus safety measures where contamination risk is highest while piped water expansion continues.

article.articleSummary: A single case in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam describes a 20-year-old with pneumonia caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) confirmed by blood culture, following a lip wound near the mouth that likely served as the entry portal. Chest CT revealed bilateral dense lung consolidations with pleural effusions and features consistent with septic emboli. After treatment, the patient recovered, pleural effusions resolved, and was discharged. The report emphasizes that MRSA pneumonia/sepsis can arise from hematogenous spread from non-respiratory infection sites (e.g., skin wounds, dental infections) rather than solely via the lower respiratory tract, and highlights the need for prompt evaluation of atypical presentations.

article.articleHeadline: When a 'Clean' Spinal Tap Deceives: Adenovirus Strikes
article.articleSummary: Four previously healthy toddlers (ages 13–26 months) at Vietnam National Children's Hospital developed fulminant, multiorgan adenovirus infection during June–December 2022. Adenovirus DNA was detected by real-time PCR in both cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and nasopharyngeal samples, indicating systemic infection with CNS involvement, even though CSF cell counts were near normal (1–3 cells/μL) and protein levels low (0.38–0.62 g/L). Neuroimaging in two cases showed bilateral frontoparietal cortical lesions in one patient and nonspecific frontoparietal subarachnoid space widening in the other, consistent with brain injury in immunocompetent children. All four required invasive mechanical ventilation; one required extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and renal replacement therapy. Marked hyperferritinemia was noted, with two clinically diagnosed with macrophage activation syndrome; HLH criteria were not fully evaluated. The report underscores that a normal-appearing spinal tap does not exclude CNS adenovirus disease and suggests immunomodulatory approaches if hyperinflammation contributes to deterioration.

article.articleHeadline: Determination to Prevent and Control Rabies
article.articleSummary: Six rabies deaths were recorded in Ho Chi Minh City in 2026 through mid-September, with four animal outbreaks detected in Long Son Commune, Tru Van Tho Commune, Phuoc Thang Ward, and Tan Hai Ward. Health facilities have treated more than 100,000 bite-and-scratch injuries from dogs and cats, a rise of about 11% versus the previous year. The city’s animal health department reports 24 communes/wards have begun capturing roaming dogs; nearly 500 dogs have been seized, including over 170 in Con Dao Special Administrative Region and more than 70 in Dong Hoa Ward. Fines of 1–2 million VND apply for not muzzling or leashing dogs or for not having a handler in public. Long Hai Commune registered 3 rabies deaths and 169 suspected bite reports, prompting intensified prevention measures, especially targeting children, and vaccination to achieve 80% herd immunity. Officials aim for zero human rabies deaths by 2030; a World Rabies Day event in Long Hai emphasized collective action with the theme “Stronger Together.”

article.articleHeadline: Nearly 50 children diagnosed with hand, foot and mouth disease; warning signs of severe illness.
article.articleSummary: Nearly 50 children diagnosed with hand, foot and mouth disease at Quang Ninh Provincial Pediatric Hospital in Vietnam, with most cases classified as level 1–2a. The outbreak involves Enterovirus-related HFMD, primarily Coxsackie A16 and Enterovirus 71 (EV71). EV71 can cause severe complications such as encephalitis, meningitis, pneumonia, and myocarditis, potentially resulting in death; initial symptoms can be subtle, and disease may progress rapidly within 24–48 hours. HFMD mainly affects children under five. Common signs include sores on hands, feet, and mouth, high fever above 39°C, irritability, vomiting, and crying; some children show minimal external signs, hindering early diagnosis. Transmission is direct person-to-person via saliva, nasal secretions, and feces. No specific antiviral exists; management is supportive. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, avoiding crowded places, isolating affected children, and monitoring for warning signs such as persistent fever, lethargy, poor feeding, drooling, tremors, or ataxia.

article.articleHeadline: Small wounds carry a risk of infection.
article.articleSummary: 11-year-old Gia Khanh from Lam Dong, Vietnam, sustained a foot abrasion after a fall while cycling. Although initially asymptomatic, the wound later swelled and he developed fever and loss of appetite, necessitating hospitalization for severe soft-tissue infection (cellulitis) of the foot and several days of antibiotics and observation. The case shows that minor-looking injuries can progress and that unmonitored or poor home care—such as herbal poultices, tobacco paste, toothpaste, or coffee on wounds—may raise infection risk. Early proper wound care is essential: clean dirty wounds with running water, remove debris, and, after animal exposure (bite, scratch, lick), rinse with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, then disinfect and seek medical evaluation for tetanus and rabies risk. Vaccination history guided care; Gia Khanh received a tetanus-containing vaccine and later completed missing doses. Parents should monitor for increasing swelling, redness, pus, fever, or reduced movement and seek care promptly.

article.articleHeadline: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 20 (21 - 27 September 2026)
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé) with 8,116 confirmed cases and 3,924 deaths (case fatality rate 48.3%) as of 27 September 2026. Across 63 health zones in 7 provinces, Ituri accounts for 76.2% of cumulative cases, maintaining its position as the outbreak epicenter; the daily number of new confirmed cases has declined but transmission persists across multiple provinces. On 27 Sept, 49 new confirmed cases and 23 deaths were reported (18 community deaths), with Ituri (27), North Kivu (18), and Haut-Uélé (4) most affected. National contact follow-up rate stands at 75.9%, highlighting ongoing challenges in surveillance, case investigation and timely care. The outbreak unfolds within a complex humanitarian and mobility context, with cross-border movements and preparedness activities in neighboring countries. IOM supports response in DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, and preparedness in Angola, CAR, Ethiopia, Kenya, Republic of the Congo, Tanzania and Zambia under IASC activation.

triage.notes: 発生地域リストには周辺国（ザンビア、ウガンダ、ルワンダ、ブルンジ、南スーダン、アンゴラ、CAR、エチオピア、ケニア、タンザニア等）が含まれるが、サマリーによればこれらは実際の発症国ではなくIOMによる準備・対応支援の対象国であるため、verified_locationsには含めず、実際にアウトブレイクが発生しているDRCのみを記載した。

article.articleHeadline: Land Border Travelers in Ghana Show Sky-High COVID-19 Antibody Levels
article.articleSummary: 92.3% of travelers entering Ghana via ten major land borders in 2022 carried SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies, according to a cross-sectional study in BMC Infectious Diseases. From February to July 2022, adults 18+ were recruited at land crossings; blood samples were analyzed with the WANTAI spike-RBD ELISA to detect antibodies blocking spike-ACE2 binding, reflecting immunity from vaccination or prior infection. Pre-border reopening seroprevalence was 95.7% (CI 94.2–97.1); after reopening it was 91.6% (CI 91.0–92.5). The pattern suggests widespread transmission by early–mid-2022 and saturation of immunity across borders. Aflao (east, high traffic) served as the immunological high-water mark; pre-opening, Oseikojokrom and Akanu had lower odds of seropositivity vs Aflao; post-opening, Elubo, Paga, and Sampa also had lower odds. Vaccinated travelers had 2.5x higher odds of neutralizing antibodies than unvaccinated before reopening. Analyses used logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q<0.05).

triage.headline_ja: ガーナの陸路国境通過者、COVID-19抗体保有率が非常に高いことが判明
triage.triage_reason: 2022年の血清疫学調査結果の報告であり、現在進行中の公衆衛生上の異常事態や新規アウトブレイクを示すものではない。疾患タグ（Coccidioidomycosis）と記事内容（COVID-19抗体）も一致しておらず、シグナルとしての緊急性は認められない。
triage.notes: 記事は2022年2-7月に実施された過去の血清有病率研究の学術論文報告であり、現在の感染症流行や公衆衛生上の脅威を示すものではない。疾患分類（Coccidioidomycosis）は誤タグの可能性が高く、実際の内容はCOVID-19抗体保有率調査。Ghanaは対象国リストに含まれるが、事象としてはトリアージ対象外と判断。
